question.text: What is 'reversal trading' in the context of fraudulent trade practices?

answer.text: A legitimate hedging strategy where positions are reversed at end of day
Reversing a trade by buying back securities sold short

Trading where connected/group entities execute reversed buy and sell transactions between themselves within close time proximity, contributing to LTP manipulation and indicating a prior meeting of minds
Selling securities after a market reversal signal

explanation.text: The Logic: Per workbook pages 153-154 (Sunita Gupta/Gangotri case), the Vishvas group executed reversal trades along with synchronized and circular trades; trades executed within a few seconds among other group entities indicated a prior meeting of minds and contributed to LTP manipulation. Page 49 supports the related no-change-of-ownership and circular-transaction fraud concepts. The Trap: Option B describes ordinary short covering, which is a legitimate trade. Option A describes day-end position management. Neither captures the coordinated, connected-party reversal pattern that the case treats as fraudulent. Note: The source emphasises connected entities, close time proximity, and LTP manipulation; treat any broader characterisation as case-specific reasoning rather than a stand-alone legal definition.
